title: Syria foreign minister sees Israel security talks resuming despite no trust
gist: Syria's foreign minister Asaad al-Shaibani says Damascus expects Israel-Syria security-deal talks to resume despite deep distrust and a recent Israeli airstrike on a Syrian airbase, revealing a near-complete 'on paper' agreement from earlier this year that stalled because Israel allegedly lacked real will to implement it.

themes.theme: Status of the Israel-Syria security deal

insights.claim: Syria and Israel had agreed on paper to almost the entirety of a security deal around the beginning of 2026 that would require Israel to stop attacking Syria and be tied to Israel's withdrawal from territory it seized after Assad's fall, but Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani says Israel then sought to evade implementation.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: A near-complete but unimplemented deal framework means any resumption of talks could move quickly to signature if political will returns, making Israel-Syria de-escalation a lower-effort, higher-probability catalyst than a deal built from scratch.
insights.quote: We did not see they had the real will to reach an agreement.
insights.locator: section 'SYRIA DID NOT SEE ISRAELI WILL TO MAKE DEAL'

insights.claim: The stalled security deal reportedly includes several security zones in Syrian territory near the Israeli border, including a buffer zone where only the United Nations would be present, and other zones where Syrian forces would deploy at varying force levels.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Concrete zone-based structure (UN buffer zone plus tiered Syrian force deployment) is the template likely to reappear if/when talks restart -- a useful reference point for tracking eventual deal terms.

insights.claim: Foreign Minister Shaibani said Syria and Israel had negotiations frozen since the start of the Iran war, with all contact cut after Israel's strike on the Abu al-Duhur airbase, but he expects talks to resume soon.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: A specific, named prediction (talks resuming 'soon') from Syria's top diplomat gives a trackable near-term catalyst for Israel-Syria de-escalation; no date was set, so treat as directional rather than time-bound.
insights.quote: I believe negotiations will resume soon.

insights.claim: Shaibani said Syria does not currently trust Israel, framing any resumed contact as conditional: if it does not bring results, Damascus does not need it.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Syria is signaling a results-based, not unconditional, willingness to engage -- suggesting any resumed dialogue will be fragile and vulnerable to breakdown at the next Israeli strike.
insights.quote: We do not trust Israel currently.

insights.claim: Israel bombed the Abu al-Duhur airbase in Syria, claiming Damascus was about to allow Turkish forces to deploy there -- a claim both Syria and Turkey denied.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: The airbase strike is the direct trigger that froze the security-deal talks; any repeat of this pattern (Israeli strikes citing Turkish deployment fears) is a leading indicator of renewed talk breakdowns.
insights.locator: section 'GOLAN HEIGHTS', reference to Tuesday strike

insights.claim: Israel seized territory in southwest Syria after Bashar al-Assad was toppled in December 2024, citing the need to safeguard its citizens, and bombed scores of Syrian military sites, with Israeli officials describing Syria's new rulers as barely disguised jihadists even as President Ahmed al-Sharaa built close US ties.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Israel's post-Assad territorial seizure and characterization of Sharaa's government as jihadist-linked is the core structural obstacle to any Israel-Syria normalization, independent of the airbase-specific dispute.

insights.claim: Shaibani argued that Israel's approach of trying to maintain security through brute force in Syria and elsewhere in the region has not succeeded anywhere.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Syria's explicit framing of Israeli military deterrence as strategically ineffective is a talking point likely to recur in Syrian diplomacy and could shape how Damascus negotiates future security terms (favoring political/UN-backed guarantees over unilateral Israeli enforcement).
insights.quote: Israel has tried to maintain its security through brute force and it hasn't succeeded

insights.claim: Washington has been trying for over a year to broker a security deal between Israel and Ahmed al-Sharaa's government, treating Syria as a new US ally in the Middle East, but the effort has proven elusive.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Confirms Washington has significant diplomatic capital invested in Syria-Israel normalization, making renewed US pressure (per Barrack) a real catalyst rather than rhetorical positioning.

insights.claim: US special envoy for Syria Tom Barrack said Washington is working to establish a mechanism to prevent conflict among Israel, Turkey and Syria, though Shaibani said there is no agreement yet on the mechanism, which he insists must stop Israeli attacks rather than entrench occupation.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: A trilateral Israel-Turkey-Syria deconfliction mechanism, if finalized, would be a significant de-escalation development for a region with two active flashpoints (Syria-Israel and Turkey-Israel); watch for Barrack's mechanism proposal to firm up.

insights.claim: Syria relies on Turkish support for military training and cooperation, as well as similar support from Jordan and Saudi Arabia, as it rebuilds its military after 14 years of war.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Maps Syria's current external military-patron network (Turkey, Jordan, Saudi Arabia), relevant context for understanding why Israel views growing Turkish influence in Syria as a specific security threat.

insights.claim: Syria and Israel have technically been in a state of war since 1948, and Israel seized the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 war; Shaibani said the priority is to stop Israeli aggression before reaching a security agreement, after which the topics of peace and the Golan could open.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Confirms the Golan Heights remains explicitly on Syria's long-term negotiating agenda, even if sequenced after an immediate security/withdrawal deal -- a longer-horizon flashpoint to track separately from the current airbase dispute.
insights.quote: Then perhaps we can open the topics of peace and the Golan.
